overview:
Anuyogadvara (Anuyogadvāra Sūtra, often written Anuyogdwar) is a Śvetāmbara Jain canonical text belonging to the group of Cūlikā Āgamas, traditionally counted as the second Cūlikā (Chulika-02) among the thirty-two principal Āgamas in the Śvetāmbara canon. It is composed in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit and is attributed, in the canonical tradition, to the Gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Lord Mahāvīra, with later redaction and transmission by early Jain elders such as Āryarakṣita Sthavira. As a Cūlikā text, it is not primarily a narrative or doctrinal treatise like the Mūla Āgamas, but a methodological and interpretive work that provides the "gateway" (dvāra) to the various modes of exposition (anuyoga) used in Jain scriptural study.

The term "anuyoga" in Jain usage refers to modes or approaches of scriptural interpretation and teaching—such as storytelling, doctrinal analysis, cosmological description, and karmic exposition. Anuyogadvara systematically explains how these approaches are to be applied to the canonical corpus. Modern editors and commentators describe it as "jaina Agamoṃ kī vyākhyā paddhati batāne vālā apanī śailī kā anūṭhā Agama"—a unique Āgama that teaches the method of commentary on Jain scriptures and can be called "Agama jñāna ke nagara kā praveśa dvāra," the gateway to the city of scriptural knowledge.

The text is structured as a series of sūtras (aphoristic statements) that are then unfolded into multiple levels of classification and sub-classification. Commentators liken this to a single drop of water expanding into an ocean of meaning and then returning to the original point: "eka sūtra ke bheda-prabheda-upabheda-avāntara bheda isa prakāra isameṃ bindu kā sindhu ke rūpa meṃ vistāra hotā pratīta hotā hai, aura anta meṃ punaḥ usī bindu para pahum̐cakara samūce viṣaya kā samavtāra kiyā jātā hai." Through this method, Anuyogadvara trains the reader to see how brief canonical statements can be systematically elaborated without losing doctrinal balance.

Among its contents, Anuyogadvara discusses: the meaning and four aspects of anuyoga; ten types of representation (sthāpanā) used in doctrinal and ritual contexts; the nature and kinds of dravya-śruta (material scripture) and dravya-skandha (material aggregates); six facets of avashyakas (essential practices); the distinction between upakrama and anugama (beginning and continuation), parikarma and vastu-vināśa (preparation and destruction of objects); bhāva-upakrama (mental beginnings) and aprasasta-bhāva-upakrama (unwholesome mental beginnings); kevalī-samudghāta (special karmic processes of omniscients); the structure of the lower worlds and seven hellish earths; tiryak-loka kṣetra-anupūrvi (gradations of the animal realm); six shapes of human bodies and five shapes of ajīva (non-sentient bodies); five types of thought-activity (cintā); the starting place of seven sounds (war); and the recognition and examples of nine rasas (emotional or experiential qualities) arising from thought-activity.

Because it focuses on interpretive tools and classifications, Anuyogadvara is especially important for understanding how later Jain scholasticism reads the canon. It shows how categories such as dravya (substance), kṣetra (space), kāla (time), bhāva (state), and paryāya (mode) are applied in scriptural exegesis. It also clarifies the distinction between jñāyaka-śarīra (the knowing body), bhavya-śarīra (the body of spiritually capable beings), and dravya-śruta (material scripture), emphasizing that written texts—whether on palm leaf, cloth, or other materials—are only one aspect of śruta and must be connected to living knowledge.

In sectarian terms, Anuyogadvara is preserved and studied primarily in the Śvetāmbara tradition, with both Mūrtipūjaka and Sthānakavāsī lineages producing illustrated and commented editions. Modern Sthānakavāsī editors such as Up-pravartak Amar Muni have prepared bilingual (Hindi–English) editions that present the mūla text, word-by-word glosses, doctrinal exposition (bhāvārtha), and interpretive essays, making the work accessible to contemporary students. While Digambara canonical lists differ and do not include Anuyogadvara as an Āgama, Digambara scholars are aware of its existence and sometimes refer to its classifications in comparative studies.

From a historical perspective, Anuyogadvara reflects the early Jain concern with preserving not only doctrinal content but also the correct method of teaching and interpreting that content. It stands at the intersection of hermeneutics, pedagogy, and doctrinal taxonomy. For students of Jainism, it offers insight into how the tradition itself conceptualizes "scriptural study" (svādhyāya) and "exposition" (pravacana), and how the four anuyogas—narrative, doctrinal, cosmological, and karmic—are woven together in a single interpretive framework.

primary_sources.title: Anuyogadvāra Sūtra (Anuyogdwar)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the Gaṇadharas; compiled in the Śvetāmbara canon; later associated with Āryarakṣita Sthavira as redactor
primary_sources.original_text: [सूत्र] से किं तं जाणगसरीर-भवियसरीर-वतिरित्तं दव्वसुयं? जाणगसरीर-भवियसरीर-वतिरित्तं दव्वसुयं–पत्तय-पोत्थय-लिहियं। अहवा सुयं पंचविहं पन्नत्तं, तं जहा–अंडयं बोंडयं कीडयं वालयं वक्कयं। से किं तं अंडयं? अंडयं–हंसगब्भाइ। से तं अंडयं। से किं तं बोंडयं? बोंडयं–फलिहमाइ। से तं बोंडयं। से किं तं कीडयं? कीडयं पंचविहं पन्नत्तं, तं जहा–पट्टे मलए अंसुए चीणंसुए किमिरागे। से तं कीडयं। से किं तं वालयं? वालयं पंचविहं पन्नत्तं, तं जहा–उन्निए उट्टिए मियलोमिए कुतवे किट्टिसे। से तं वालयं। से किं तं वक्कयं? वक्कयं–सणमाइ। से तं वक्कयं। से तं जाणगसरीर-भवियसरीर-वतिरित्तं दव्वसुयं। से तं नोआगमओ दव्वसुयं। से तं दव्वसुयं।
primary_sources.transliteration: [sutra] se kim tam janagasarira-bhaviyasarira-vatirittam davvasuyam? janagasarira-bhaviyasarira-vatirittam davvasuyam–pattaya-potthaya-lihiyam. ahava suyam pamchaviham pannattam, tam jaha–amdayam bomdayam kidayam valayam vakkayam. se kim tam amdayam? amdayam–hamsagabbhai. se tam amdayam. se kim tam bomdayam? bomdayam–phalihamai. se tam bomdayam. se kim tam kidayam? kidayam pamchaviham pannattam, tam jaha–patte malae amsue chinamsue kimirage. se tam kidayam. se kim tam valayam? valayam pamchaviham pannattam, tam jaha–unnie uttie miyalomie kutave kittise. se tam valayam. se kim tam vakkayam? vakkayam–sanamai. se tam vakkayam. se tam janagasarira-bhaviyasarira-vatirittam davvasuyam. se tam noagamao davvasuyam. se tam davvasuyam.
primary_sources.translation:
Sūtra: What is the dravya-śruta (material scripture) that is other than the knowing body and the body of the spiritually capable (bhavya) beings? The dravya-śruta that is other than the knowing body and the bhavya body is the scripture written on palm leaves or sheets gathered in the form of a book. Or, it is said to be of five kinds: egg-born (aṇḍaja), cotton-born (boṇḍaja), insect-produced (kīṭaja), hair-produced (vālaja), and bark-produced (valkaja).

What is egg-born? Egg-born is the thread (sūtra) made from the womb of the swan (hamsa-garbha) and similar. That is called egg-born. What is cotton-born? Cotton-born is the thread made from cotton or fluff. That is called cotton-born. What is insect-produced? Insect-produced is said to be of five kinds: cloth (paṭṭa), Malaya cloth, Aṃśuka, Chinese cloth, and cloth colored by insects (kṛmi-rāga). That is called insect-produced. What is hair-produced? Hair-produced is said to be of five kinds: woolen (aurṇika), camel-hair (auṣṭrika), deer-hair (mṛga-lomika), and other such varieties like kautava and kiṭṭisa. That is called hair-produced. What is bark-produced? Bark-produced is thread made from hemp and similar fibers. That is called bark-produced. This is the dravya-śruta that is other than the knowing body and the bhavya body. This is the non-newly arisen (non-recent) dravya-śruta. This is dravya-śruta.
primary_sources.notes: This passage, preserved in Ardhamāgadhī and transmitted in Śvetāmbara editions of Anuyogadvāra Sūtra, defines dravya-śruta (material scripture) as the physical written form of teachings, distinguishing it from the living cognitive embodiment of knowledge. It classifies scriptural materials according to the origin of the writing thread or medium—palm leaf, cotton, insect-produced silk, wool, and bark fibers—illustrating the text’s concern with precise categorization. The closing statement emphasizes that such written scripture is distinct from the knowing body and the bhavya body, and that it is an established, not newly arisen, form of dravya-śruta. This reflects the hermeneutical orientation of Anuyogadvāra, which carefully distinguishes material and cognitive aspects of scripture.

primary_sources.transliteration: anuyoga dvāra sūtra jaina Agamoṃ kī vyākhyā paddhati batāne vālā apanī śailī kā anūṭhā Agama hai. ise Agama jñāna ke nagara kā praveśa dvāra kahā jā sakatā hai. eka prācīna dohe meṃ kahā hai: jyoṃ kele ke pāta meṃ, pāta-pāta meṃ pāta; tyoṃ jñānī kī bāta meṃ, bāta-bāta meṃ bāta. anuyoga dvāra ke viṣaya meṃ yaha sūkti yathārtha lagatī hai. eka sūtra ke bheda-prabheda-upabheda-avāntara bheda isa prakāra isameṃ bindu kā sindhu ke rūpa meṃ vistāra hotā pratīta hotā hai, aura anta meṃ punaḥ usī bindu para pahum̐cakara samūce viṣaya kā samavatāra kiyā jātā hai. tattvavivecana kī sārthaka aura saṃtulita paddhati ke anusāra isa sūtra meṃ vividha viṣayoṃ kā vistāra ke sātha varṇana hai. isa Agama kā abhyāsa karane para prācīna dharmagranthoṃ kī varṇana śailī sahaja hī samajha meṃ ā sakatī hai.
primary_sources.translation: Anuyog-dvar Sutra is a unique Scripture that explains the method of detailed interpretation of Jain Agams in its own style. It can be called the gateway of the City of Agamic knowledge. A Hindi couplet aptly applies to the subject matter of Anuyog-dvar: just as in the leaf of a banana tree there are leaves within leaves, so in the word of a seer there are meanings within meanings. This saying is truly appropriate to the subject of Anuyog-dvar. One Sutra has many divisions, sub-divisions and further divisions; in this way, in it a point seems to expand into an ocean, and in the end, again arriving at that very point, the entire subject is summarized. Following a meaningful and balanced style for the analysis of tattvas (fundamental principles), this Sutra describes many topics in detail. By studying this Scripture, the style of description in ancient religious texts can easily be understood.
primary_sources.notes: This modern Hindi–English introduction, prepared in a Sthānakavāsī edition, is not itself part of the ancient Ardhamāgadhī mūla but reflects a traditional understanding of Anuyogadvāra’s function. It emphasizes the text’s role as a hermeneutical gateway and uses a poetic analogy to describe the layered nature of scriptural meaning. The passage also highlights the pedagogical value of Anuyogadvāra for understanding the style of older Jain scriptures. As a secondary but tradition-aware source, it belongs to corpus tier B–C (reviewed commentary and scholarship) and should be read alongside the primary Prakrit text.

misconceptions.myth: Anuyogadvara is a minor or purely technical text that has little relevance for ordinary lay practitioners.
misconceptions.reality: While Anuyogadvāra Sūtra is indeed technical in its classifications and interpretive methods, it plays a central role in shaping how Jain teachings are understood and communicated. Its explanations of anuyoga, dravya-śruta, avashyakas, and other categories inform sermons, study practices, and doctrinal expositions that reach lay audiences. For students and serious lay practitioners, it offers valuable insight into the structure of Jain thought and the way scriptural study is traditionally organized.

misconceptions.myth: Anuyogadvara belongs only to one sub-sect (for example, Sthānakavāsī) and is not part of the wider Śvetāmbara tradition.
misconceptions.reality: Anuyogadvāra is a Śvetāmbara canonical text classified as Chulika-02 in the broader Śvetāmbara Āgama list. Both Mūrtipūjaka and Sthānakavāsī lineages preserve and study it, and multiple editions—illustrated, commented, and bilingual—have been produced across Śvetāmbara communities. Sthānakavāsī editors have contributed influential modern commentaries, but the text itself is not sect-exclusive within the Śvetāmbara tradition.

misconceptions.myth: Because Anuyogadvara discusses material scripture (dravya-śruta), it reduces scripture to physical books and neglects the living transmission of knowledge.
misconceptions.reality: The sūtras that define dravya-śruta explicitly distinguish material scripture from the knowing body (jñāyaka-śarīra) and the bhavya body, indicating that written texts are only one aspect of śruta. Anuyogadvāra’s careful classification of writing materials serves to clarify the physical basis of scripture, not to deny the importance of oral, cognitive, and experiential transmission. In Jain hermeneutics, both dravya-śruta (material scripture) and bhāva-śruta (scripture as lived and understood) are necessary and complementary.
